title: The Light Thief: Why Transition-Metal Ions Are Coloured
subject: Chemistry
objective: Ligands split the five d orbitals of a transition-metal ion into a lower and an upper level. A d electron absorbs the one band of visible light whose energy equals the gap and jumps up (a d–d transition); the rest of the light reaches the eye, so we see the complementary colour: Ti³⁺(aq) eats green-yellow and looks purple, Cu²⁺(aq) eats red-orange and looks blue. The ligand sets the gap (ruby and emerald are both Cr³⁺), and d⁰ / d¹⁰ ions such as Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ are colourless.

fill.q: The colour of transition-metal ions arises from ____ transitions.
The colour we see is the ____ colour of the light absorbed.
The frequency of light absorbed is determined by the nature of the ____.
Sc³⁺ (Z of Sc = 21) has ____ d electrons, so it is colourless.
Zn²⁺ (Z of Zn = 30) has ____ d electrons, so it is colourless.
In a free ion the five d orbitals have ____ energy.

tf.q: Cu²⁺(aq) is blue because it absorbs blue light.
tf.explain: It absorbs red-orange light; blue is the complementary colour that is transmitted.

tf.q: Ligands split the d orbitals into two sets of different energy.
tf.explain: With six ligands: three lower, two upper.
Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰: no d electron, so no d–d transition.

tf.q: The energy absorbed in a d–d transition usually lies in the visible region.
The same metal ion always has the same colour, whatever its ligands.
tf.explain: Cr³⁺ is red in ruby and green in emerald; the ligand sets the gap.

ar.r: Zn²⁺ has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ configuration.
ar.explain: No empty d orbital above, so no d–d transition.
The reason is false: it absorbs red-orange; blue is what remains.

mcq.q: Which ion is colourless in water?
A solution absorbs green-yellow light. Its colour is:
Which configuration cannot show a d–d transition?
mcq.explain: No vacancy in the d orbitals.

mcq.q: In a d–d transition the electron moves:
mcq.explain: Lower d set → upper d set.

num.q: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs most strongly near 500 nm. Use E = 1240/λ(nm) eV to find the energy gap.
Ruby's gap is about 2.23 eV and emerald's about 2.05 eV. Find the wavelength each absorbs most (λ = 1240/E).

short.q: Explain why Ti³⁺(aq) is coloured but Ti⁴⁺(aq) is colourless.
short.solution: Ti³⁺ is 3d¹: its one d electron can absorb visible light and jump from the lower to the upper d level (d–d transition); the complementary colour (purple) is seen. Ti⁴⁺ is 3d⁰: no d electron, no d–d transition, no visible absorption.

short.q: What is meant by complementary colour? Give one example from transition-metal ions.
short.solution: The colour that remains when one band is removed from white light (opposite on the colour wheel). Cu²⁺(aq) absorbs red-orange and looks blue.

short.q: Ruby and emerald both contain Cr³⁺. Why do they have different colours?
short.solution: The surroundings (ligand field) of Cr³⁺ differ: ruby's d-orbital gap is larger, so it absorbs yellow-green and looks red; emerald's gap is smaller, so it absorbs red-orange and looks green.
